catalog_quote: Zaar has a three-tier tone system: H (marked with an acute accent: á), M (unmarked: a), L (marked with a grave accent: à). Initial nonimplosive voiced obstruents have a depressor effect on tones in a some grammatical environments ... L tone tends to spread over M clitics (tonal sandhi). ... Zaar has two verb tone classes: Middle (M) and High (H), which can be contrasted in the Perfective. ... The role of pitch in Zaar intonation can be observed in the variation between lexical and grammatical tones as they are perceived and transcribed by the native speaker and their acoustic realization.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Zaar is described as a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus contour tones and depressor-consonant effects, verb tone classes M and H); the grammar has no section on word stress or accent and makes no statement about stress placement or its absence.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement); tonal detail only: depressor effect of initial non-implosive voiced obstruents, L spreading onto M clitics, floating H of the genitive link, verb tone classes.
new_statements.identity_note: Zaːr proper (Sayanci 'of Kal' and neighbouring villages, Tafawa Balewa LGA, Bauchi State), the variety of Caron's fieldwork since 1991; not the Sigidi/Guus or Zakshi dialects also grouped under saya1246.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in the held Caron sketch at the stated sections/pages; two further held Caron primaries (2005 dictionary-grammar, 2015 Tone and Intonation) and two newly downloaded Caron intonation papers all describe Zaar as a three-tone language (H/M/L + F/R contours, depressor consonants, grammatical tone) with no word-stress or accent rule, and the 2015 Benjamins chapter explicitly contrasts Zaar's 'tone system' with lexical-stress and pitch accent systems elsewhere in Afroasiatic. Caron is the principal describer; no reference grammar exists per Glottolog. The one unheld higher-type source, Schneeberg 1974 Sayanci Phonology (diss.), is the basis Caron cites and is unlikely to overturn a 'tonal, no stress rule described' coding; listed as a medium-priority works still to obtain only.

The intonation of Topic and Focus: Zaar (Nigeria), Tamasheq (Niger), Juba Arabic (South Sudan) and Tripoli Arabic (Libya). In A. Mettouchi, M. Vanhove & D. Caubet (eds.), Corpus-based Studies of Lesser-described Languages: The CorpAfroAs corpus of spoken AfroAsiatic languages (Studies in Corpus Linguistics 68), 63-115. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. HAL halshs-00922747.
sources.quote: 'Afroasiatic languages have phonologized pitch into different prosodic systems that vary from a demarcative accent system, e.g. Berber; to a lexical stress system, e.g. Tripoli Arabic; a pitch accent system, e.g. Juba Arabic; and a tone system, e.g. Hausa and Zaar' (p. 2); 'Zaar is a tone language with three phonemic tones: High ... Mid ... Low. Two contour tones result from the combinations High-Mid and Low-Mid on a single syllable' (p. 5); 'There is no intensity stress on the focus' (p. 10).
sources.locator: HAL p. 2 (introduction); p. 5 sec. 2.1 'Zaar prosodic system'; p. 10 (focus)

sources.citation: Caron, Bernard. 2013. The intonation of Topic and Focus in Zaar (Chadic, SBW). Conference paper, HAL halshs-00922387, 15 pp.
sources.quote: Treats Zaar throughout as a tone language; 'There is no intensity stress on the focus, or pause between the left-dislocated focus and the predication.' No word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Caron, Bernard (2011). Tonal Inversion in Geji and Pelu.
sources.note: Describes Geji and Pelu (Geji language, gejj1241-type variety, not Zaar). It only places Zaar in the South Bauchi West family tree; nothing on Zaar word stress.

The catalog record for Zaar has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this work gives no word-stress statement, only the tone system (3 levels + 2 contours), so it neither confirms nor contradicts anything. It confirms Zaar is a tone language.

Nothing specific to Zeem proper; no TBU/downstep discussion.
